name: LM2594M-ADJ_NOPB
title: LM2594, LM2594HV: 0.5 A, 150 kHz step-down switching regulator, 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and adjustable
summary: A monolithic buck regulator that switches an internal power transistor at a fixed 150 kHz with its loop compensation on chip, so a complete supply takes only an input capacitor, a catch diode, an inductor and an output capacitor. It delivers 0.5 A from 4.5 V to 40 V in (LM2594) or to 60 V in (LM2594HV), in fixed 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions and an adjustable version referenced to 1.23 V (1.2 V to 37 V out, 57 V for the HV). An active-low ON/OFF pin cuts the supply current to about 85 µA, and a two-stage current limit and thermal shutdown protect it. It comes in 8-pin SOIC (D) and PDIP (P); the LM2594M-ADJ/NOPB is the 40 V adjustable version in SOIC, in tubes of 95.

pins.function: Closes the regulation loop by sensing the output: wired to the output on the fixed versions, to the R1/R2 divider tap on the adjustable version.

pins.function: Active-low shutdown. Below roughly 1.3 V the regulator runs; above it (up to 25 V) the regulator stops and the input current falls to about 80 µA. Grounded or left open, the regulator is on.

pins.function: Supply input. An input bypass capacitor at this pin holds down voltage transients and supplies the pulsed switch current.

pins.name: Output
pins.function: The internal switch: it swings between about +VIN − VSAT and about −0.5 V at a duty cycle of VOUT / VIN. Copper on this node is kept small to limit coupling into nearby circuits.

circuits.title: Typical application, fixed output version
circuits.description: The 5 V version stepping an unregulated 12 V supply down to 5 V for a 0.5 A load. The switch on the Output pin chops the input; L1 and COUT filter the pulses into a steady output, and D1 carries the inductor current during the off time. Feedback is wired straight to the output and ON/OFF to ground, so the converter always runs. CIN holds the input up against the switch current pulses.

circuits.title: Fixed output voltage versions (Figure 9-10)
circuits.description: The basic buck circuit for the 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions. The Output pin drives L1 and the catch diode D1; COUT smooths the output, which returns to Feedback over its own wire. ON/OFF is grounded so the regulator is always on. The input capacitor, the regulator ground, the diode anode and the output capacitor return all sit on one short ground. For inputs of 40 V to 60 V on the LM2594HV the parts need higher voltage ratings.

parts.note: 35 V aluminum electrolytic, Nichicon PL series
25 V aluminum electrolytic, Nichicon PL series

notes: The wires from CIN, the Ground pin, D1 and COUT carry the switched currents and are kept short over a ground plane.
The feedback wire is routed away from the inductor's magnetic field.

circuits.title: Optional post ripple filter (Figure 9-10)
circuits.description: A second LC stage after the converter's output for output ripple below about 15 mV: a 3 µH series inductor and a 100 µF low-ESR capacitor on short leads. It is outside the feedback loop, so its capacitor's ESR may be as low as wanted.

circuits.title: Adjustable output voltage version, 20 V design example (Figure 9-13)
circuits.description: The adjustable version set for 20 V out from inputs up to 28 V at 0.5 A. R1 and R2 divide the output down to the 1.23 V feedback reference at the Feedback pin: R2 = 1 kΩ × (20 / 1.23 − 1) gives 15.26 kΩ, rounded to 15.4 kΩ. CFF across R2 adds loop stability, which outputs above about 10 V need. L1, D1, CIN and COUT are the values the design procedure picks for 20 V out and 28 V in. ON/OFF is grounded.

parts.note: 50 V, Panasonic HFQ series; or 120 µF, 50 V, Nichicon PL series

notes: As the general adjustable circuit (the test circuit of the electrical characteristics), the parts are CIN 68 µF 35 V and COUT 120 µF 25 V, both Nichicon PL electrolytics, L1 100 µH (L20), D1 1N5819, R1 1 kΩ 1 %, R2 from the output voltage equation and CFF from Table 9-7.
R1 and R2 sit close to the Feedback pin on short leads, and the feedback wiring stays away from the inductor.

circuits.title: Delayed start-up (Figure 8-1)
circuits.description: Keeps the regulator off for a time after the input comes up. While VIN is rising, C1 drives current through R1 into the ON/OFF node and holds it high, so the switch stays off; once VIN is steady, R2 pulls ON/OFF low and switching starts. R1 caps the ON/OFF voltage below its 25 V limit, lowers noise pickup and limits C1's discharge current. Output and Feedback connect as in the basic buck circuit. The delay lets a current-limited source rise further before the regulator loads it.
notes: A long delay is avoided when the input carries large ripple, since the ripple couples onto ON/OFF.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for buck regulator (Figure 8-2)
circuits.description: Holds a buck regulator off until the input passes a set level. R2 pulls ON/OFF up to VIN, which keeps the part off. When VIN climbs past the 12 V Zener voltage plus Q1's base-emitter drop, current through R1 and Z1 turns Q1 on; Q1 pulls ON/OFF low and the regulator starts. R3 holds Q1 off below the threshold. The rest of the converter connects as in the basic circuit.
notes: With a Zener above 25 V, a 47 kΩ resistor from ON/OFF to the ground pin keeps ON/OFF within its 25 V limit.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for inverting regulator (Figure 8-3)
circuits.description: A lockout for the inverting circuit, whose regulator ground is the −5 V output. R1 and R2 with the 12 V Zener Z1 to system ground set the trip point at the base of the PNP Q1; Q1 then drives R3 and R4 to turn on Q2, which pulls ON/OFF down to the regulator's ground and lets it run. R5 holds ON/OFF high otherwise. The turn-on and turn-off threshold is the same, about 13 V. D1 feeds the input. The rest of the converter connects as in the basic circuit.
notes: R2's lower end connects only to Z1's cathode, not to the −5 V output.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout with hysteresis for inverting regulator (Figure 8-4)
circuits.description: The Zener-and-transistor lockout returned to the −5 V rail of the inverting circuit, which gives hysteresis roughly equal to the output voltage: switching begins at VIN = 13 V and stops at VIN = 8 V. Z1 and R1 drive Q1's base from VIN; Q1 pulls ON/OFF to the regulator's ground. R2 pulls ON/OFF up, R3 holds Q1 off. D1 feeds the input. The rest of the converter connects as in the basic circuit.

circuits.title: Inverting −5 V regulator with delayed start-up (Figure 8-5)
circuits.description: Makes −5 V from a +4.5 V to +20 V input with a common ground. The regulator's Ground pin sits on the negative output and Feedback goes to system ground, so the part regulates the inverted output. L1 returns to system ground and D2 is the catch diode. D1 blocks input ripple from reaching the output through CIN at light load and makes the loop behave like a buck. D3 keeps the output from being pulled more than a diode drop positive while CIN charges at power-up. C1, R1 and R2 delay start-up so CIN charges further before the large start-up current flows.

parts.note: 25 V tantalum, Sprague 595D; or 120 µF, 35 V electrolytic, Panasonic HFQ
20 V tantalum, Sprague 595D; or 39 µF, 16 V electrolytic, Panasonic HFQ

notes: The regulator sees |VIN| + |VOUT| between its input and ground pins, which is kept to 40 V or less; +20 V to −12 V puts 32 V across it.
A 100 µH, 1 A inductor suits most inverting designs.

circuits.title: Inverting regulator ground referenced shutdown (Figure 8-7)
circuits.description: On/off control of an inverting regulator from a logic signal referred to system ground. A shutdown input at 0 V runs the regulator: the PNP Q1, base grounded, is off and R1 holds ON/OFF at the −5 V rail. Raising the input to +V turns Q1 on through R4, lifting ON/OFF above its threshold and stopping the regulator. D1 feeds the input.
notes: Q1's emitter connects only to R4, not to VIN.

circuits.title: Inverting regulator ground referenced shutdown using opto device (Figure 8-8)
circuits.description: Ground-referred on/off control of an inverting regulator through an opto-isolator. R1 from VIN and R2 to the −5 V rail bias ON/OFF high, so with the shutdown input at 0 V the regulator is off. Driving the input to +5 V lights the LED through R3; the phototransistor pulls ON/OFF to the regulator's ground and the regulator runs. Input range +4.5 V to +25 V.

operation.text: A non-synchronous buck converter on one chip: power switch, 150 kHz oscillator, reference, error amplifier with internal compensation, current limit and thermal limit. It handles 0.5 A of load. The LM2594 runs from up to 40 V (45 V absolute maximum); the LM2594HV runs from up to 60 V. Fixed 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions and an adjustable version (1.2 V to 37 V out, 57 V for the HV) share one pinout, and a working supply needs four external parts: input capacitor, catch diode, inductor and output capacitor.

Feedback enters an internal divider with R1 = 2.5 kΩ to ground. R2 is 4.2 kΩ on the 3.3 V version, 7.6 kΩ on the 5 V and 21.8 kΩ on the 12 V. On the adjustable version R2 is 0 Ω and R1 is open. The internal reference is 1.235 V.
Output voltage holds within ±4 % across the full input range and load range, and the oscillator frequency within ±15 %.

Pulling ON/OFF below 1.3 V (at 25 °C, measured from the Ground pin) runs the regulator; taking it above 1.3 V shuts it down to a standby current of about 85 µA typ. Over temperature, 0.6 V or less is guaranteed on and 2 V or more guaranteed off. The pin accepts up to 25 V. Left open or tied to ground, the regulator is on. In an inverting circuit Ground sits at the negative output, so a ground-referred control signal needs a level shift (Figures 8-7 and 8-8).

The switch has a two-stage current limit; the second stage lowers the switching frequency, by more as the overload deepens. Peak current limit is 0.8 A typ (0.65 A to 1.3 A at 25 °C). An overtemperature shutdown completes the protection, and power dissipation is internally limited.

A capacitor from VIN to ON/OFF through a resistor, with a second resistor from ON/OFF to ground, holds the regulator off while the input rises and lets it start once the input settles (Figure 8-1). This lets a current-limited source reach a higher voltage first, where a buck draws less input current. The series resistor keeps ON/OFF under 25 V, reduces noise sensitivity and limits the capacitor's discharge current. Input ripple couples into ON/OFF, so long delays are avoided when ripple is high.

A Zener and transistor on ON/OFF keep the regulator off until the input passes a chosen level (Figure 8-2 for buck). For the inverting circuit, Figure 8-3 turns on and off at the same point, about the Zener voltage plus 1 V (about 13 V with a 12 V Zener), and Figure 8-4 adds hysteresis about equal to the output voltage (starts at 13 V, stops at 8 V). With Zeners above 25 V, an extra 47 kΩ from ON/OFF to the Ground pin keeps the pin inside its 25 V limit.

Tying the Ground pin to the negative output and Feedback to system ground makes a positive-to-negative converter (Figure 8-5); any output version can be used. Output current depends strongly on input and output voltage (Figure 8-6). The regulator sees the sum of the input and output magnitudes, kept to 40 V on the LM2594 and 60 V on the LM2594HV. D1 at the input keeps input noise from coupling through CIN to the output at light load and makes the loop behave like a buck; a Schottky suits low input voltages, a fast-recovery diode higher ones. D3 stops CIN's charging current pulling the output more than a diode drop positive at power-up. The usual inductor selection does not apply: 100 µH, 1 A suits most designs, and the Figure 8-5 capacitors suit most. Start-up draws input current up to the current limit (about 0.8 A) for 2 ms or more, depending on output voltage and output capacitance, so a source that cannot supply it will not start the circuit; the delayed start-up network is used, and CIN can be made much larger for hard starts.

The selection guides size the inductor for continuous conduction. For loads of 200 mA or less, particularly from a high input voltage, a design that runs discontinuous needs only a third to a half as much inductance, in a physically smaller part; its peak switch current is higher but stays under the current limit. In discontinuous operation the Output pin rings in a damped sine wave while neither switch nor diode conducts; this is normal and not loop instability. Ferrite cores ring most, powdered iron less, and a series RC across the inductor damps it. Lightly loaded, most designs run discontinuous whatever the inductor.

A low-ESR aluminum or tantalum capacitor between +VIN and Ground, close to the part on short leads, is required. It is chosen for RMS current rating first: about half the DC load current for ambients to 40 °C, about 75 % for up to 70 °C, and in the design procedures at least half the load current. The voltage rating is at least 1.25 times the maximum input in the general rule, about 1.5 times in the design procedures. Solid tantalum input capacitors should be surge-current tested; series resistance or inductance, or a higher voltage part, limits inrush. With ceramic input capacitors the VIN pin can ring badly. Figure 9-1 gives typical RMS ratings of low-ESR electrolytics.

Switching-grade electrolytic or solid tantalum parts with low ESR filter the output and keep the loop stable. ESR is the key parameter and has a window: low enough for the wanted ripple (typically 1 % to 2 % of VOUT), not so low that the loop oscillates. Most designs use 82 µF to 220 µF electrolytic or 15 µF to 100 µF tantalum, and nothing above 220 µF. Higher-voltage electrolytics have lower ESR, so a part rated well above 1.5 times VOUT is often used for low ripple. Electrolytic ESR roughly triples at −25 °C and can reach ten times at −40 °C, so tantalum is used below −25 °C. Tables 9-1 and 9-7 list output and feedforward capacitors by output voltage.

The diode carries the inductor current while the switch is off and sits close to the part on short traces. Schottky diodes are best, especially at 5 V and below; ultra-fast recovery rectifiers (50 ns or less) also work, though types that turn off abruptly may bring instability or EMI. 1N4001-class rectifiers are too slow and are not used. The current rating is at least 1.3 times the maximum load, or the full current limit if the output must survive a sustained short; its reverse voltage rating is 1.25 × VIN(max) or more. Table 9-2 lists suitable 1 A parts.

The nomographs of Figures 9-5 to 9-8 pick an inductor for continuous conduction, letting the peak-to-peak ripple current be a larger share of the load at light loads (Figure 9-4) to keep the inductor small. Exceeding the inductor's current rating overheats it or saturates the core; a saturating inductor turns resistive, the switch current rises fast into the cycle-by-cycle limit, output current falls and both inductor and regulator can overheat. Table 9-3 lists Schott, Renco, Pulse Engineering and Coilcraft parts by code L1 to L27.

Continuous-mode ripple is a sawtooth at the switching frequency, set by the inductor ripple current and the output capacitor's ESR, typically 0.5 % to 3 % of VOUT, with short spikes at its peaks from the fast switching edges, capacitor inductance and wiring. For ripple below 15 mV a post filter of 1 µH to 5 µH (low DC resistance) and a low-ESR capacitor follows the output; being outside the loop, its capacitor's ESR can be as low as wanted. Ripple is measured with a very short probe ground at the output capacitor rather than the usual long ground lead. Figure 9-9 gives the ripple current range by load when the selection guides are used; in the 5 V, 300 mA example with 15 V in (11 V to 20 V), ΔIIND is about 150 mA, ranging from 120 mA to 175 mA.

Bobbin and stick inductors leak flux through the air, which induces voltages in nearby traces and can raise ripple or upset the loop. If an open-core inductor seems to cause instability, lifting it several inches off the board shows whether its flux is to blame; a closed-core toroid or E-core, or a new layout, cures it. Flux through the ground trace, feedback trace or output capacitor traces is kept to a minimum; a trace exactly centred under a bobbin can be fine, and even winding direction can matter.

For a 5 V output, 12 V maximum input and 0.4 A load: the 5 V selection guide (Figure 9-6) gives 100 µH, code L20, from Table 9-3. Table 9-5 at 0.5 A and 15 V suggests 120 µF, 25 V electrolytics (Panasonic HFQ or Nichicon PL); output capacitor ratings start at 1.5 times VOUT, and a 16 V or 25 V part roughly halves the ripple of a 10 V one, which can show about 400 mΩ ESR. A 1N5817 (1 A, 20 V) is not overstressed even into a short. CIN: rated over 18 V (25 V used) and at least 200 mA RMS, so 47 µF or 68 µF at 25 V; tantalum for surface mount (AVX TPS, Sprague 593D, both surge tested).

For 20 V out, 28 V maximum input and 0.5 A: R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 15.4 kΩ; E × T = 35.2 V × µs, giving 150 µH (L19) in Figure 9-8; output capacitor 82 µF, 50 V (Panasonic HFQ) or 120 µF, 50 V (Nichicon PL), rated at least 1.5 times VOUT with 50 V chosen for lower ESR; CFF 1 nF from Table 9-7; D1 a 1N5819 (1 A, 40 V); CIN rated over 42 V, so 50 V, and 47 µF for at least 200 mA RMS.

Fast-switching currents in wiring inductance create voltage spikes, so the heavy-current paths are wide and short, with the external parts close to the regulator over a ground plane or single-point ground. Open-core inductors are placed so their flux misses the feedback, IC ground and COUT wiring. On the adjustable version both feedback resistors sit near the IC and their wiring runs away from the inductor. The Output (switch) node keeps a small copper area.

Both packages have a copper lead frame and use the board as their heat sink: wide traces, and ground and unused pins soldered to generous copper such as a ground plane, but not on the Output pin. Double-sided or multilayer boards help; sockets add thermal resistance and are avoided unless power is small. Junction temperature depends on board size, copper area and thickness, nearby heat sources such as the catch diode, and the inductor, which can draw heat away or add it. Figures 9-18 and 9-19 give the typical junction rise at 500 mA on 4 in² of single-sided 2 oz copper.
The input supply is well regulated and able to deliver the maximum input current without sagging, up to 45 V for the LM2594 and 60 V for the LM2594HV.
